items.stem: If there is a negative externality of production, which of the following is true?
items.answer: MSC > MPC
items.markingKey: D. External costs are added to private costs.

items.stem: Explain why the demand curve can be treated as the MPB curve.
items.answer: Consumers are willing to pay up to the extra benefit they gain from one more unit, so the price on the demand curve at each quantity measures their marginal private benefit.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Consumers are willing to pay up to the extra benefit they gain from one more unit, so the price on the demand curve at each quantity measures their marginal private benefit. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Leila writes: "Market failure means that a market has collapsed and nothing is sold." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Market failure means resources are misallocated – too much or too little is produced relative to the social optimum – even though the market may be very active.
items.markingKey: Market failure means resources are misallocated – too much or too little is produced relative to the social optimum – even though the market may be very active. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For cement production near a town, MPB = MSB is P = 100 − Q and MPC is P = 20 + Q (P in $, Q in thousand units). Production creates a constant external cost of $6 per unit. Calculate the market output, the socially optimal output and the welfare loss.
items.answer: Market Q = 40; optimum Q = 37; welfare loss = 9 ($ thousand)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Hypothetical estimates for a city show that each extra tonne of waste burned in an incinerator costs the operator $40 (MPC), while nearby residents suffer health and property damage estimated at $25 per tonne.
— Hypothetical data

Using the data, calculate the marginal social cost per tonne and explain why the market may burn too much waste.
items.answer: MSC = 40 + 25 = $65 per tonne; the operator decides using only the $40 private cost, so it burns where MPB = MPC, beyond the optimum where MSB = MSC = $65.
items.markingKey: MSC = 40 + 25 = $65 per tonne; the operator decides using only the $40 private cost, so it burns where MPB = MPC, beyond the optimum where MSB = MSC = $65. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Sana writes: "When MSC is greater than MPC, the market produces too little." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: When MSC > MPC (negative production externality), the market over-produces because producers ignore the external cost.
items.markingKey: When MSC > MPC (negative production externality), the market over-produces because producers ignore the external cost. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Market failure is so common that governments should intervene in most markets.
items.answer: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: externalities are widespread (energy, transport, food); information problems in health, finance. Arguments against: many markets work well without intervention; government failure is also common; intervention has administrative costs. Supported judgement: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that the concept of allocative efficiency (MSB = MSC) is of limited practical use because external costs cannot be measured accurately.
items.answer: Measurement is difficult, but the MSB = MSC framework remains essential for deciding the direction and approximate scale of intervention.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: external costs (health, climate) are hard to value in money; estimates vary widely (social cost of carbon). Arguments against: even approximate values improve policy (carbon prices); the framework shows the direction of correction; cost-benefit analysis is widely used. Judgement: Measurement is difficult, but the MSB = MSC framework remains essential for deciding the direction and approximate scale of intervention. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "marginal social benefit (MSB)".
items.answer: The extra benefit to society from one more unit, equal to MPB plus any marginal external benefit
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the extra benefit to society from one more unit, equal to MPB plus any marginal external benefit. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why welfare loss arises when output exceeds the socially optimal level.
items.answer: Beyond the optimum, each extra unit has MSC > MSB: society values it less than it costs, so producing it subtracts from social surplus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Beyond the optimum, each extra unit has MSC > MSB: society values it less than it costs, so producing it subtracts from social surplus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Market failure means resources are misallocated – too much or too little is produced relative to the social optimum – even though the market may be very active.
items.markingKey: Market failure means resources are misallocated – too much or too little is produced relative to the social optimum – even though the market may be very active. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline why a free market fails to achieve allocative efficiency when there is a negative externality of production.
items.answer: Diagram: MPB = MSB (demand), MPC (supply) and MSC above MPC. Market output Qm where MPB = MPC at price Pm; social optimum Q* where MSB = MSC. Qm > Q*: over-allocation of resources; welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Qm.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: MPB = MSB (demand), MPC (supply) and MSC above MPC. Market output Qm where MPB = MPC at price Pm; social optimum Q* where MSB = MSC. Qm > Q*: over-allocation of resources; welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Qm. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Which of the following is a negative externality of consumption?
options: Bees from a beekeeper pollinating orchards
Noise from a neighbour's late-night party
items.answer: Noise from a neighbour's late-night party
items.markingKey: D. The harm results from consumption and affects third parties.

items.stem: Explain why taxes on negative externalities are difficult to set at the correct level.
items.answer: The marginal external cost is hard to measure in money terms (health, environment), varies by location and over time, so the tax may be too high or too low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The marginal external cost is hard to measure in money terms (health, environment), varies by location and over time, so the tax may be too high or too low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a carbon tax and a cap-and-trade (tradable permit) scheme.
items.answer: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the price of permits adjust in the market.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the price of permits adjust in the market. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

The EU Emissions Trading System covers around 40% of EU greenhouse gas emissions. The price of an allowance rose from under €10 per tonne in 2017 to over €90 in 2022 after the EU tightened the cap. Emissions from power generation fell sharply as coal plants closed.
— Extract based on reporting of the EU ETS

Using the extract, explain how tradable permits help to reduce a negative externality.
items.answer: The cap limits total emissions; firms must buy allowances, so emitting becomes costly; a tighter cap raised the permit price, giving firms the incentive to cut emissions (e.g. close coal plants) – the externality is internalised.
items.markingKey: The cap limits total emissions; firms must buy allowances, so emitting becomes costly; a tighter cap raised the permit price, giving firms the incentive to cut emissions (e.g. close coal plants) – the externality is internalised. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Identify one negative externality of production and one of consumption associated with fast fashion.
items.answer: Production: water pollution and emissions from textile factories; consumption: textile waste in landfill (or microplastic shedding when washing).
items.markingKey: Production: water pollution and emissions from textile factories; consumption: textile waste in landfill (or microplastic shedding when washing).

items.stem: Using Sweden's carbon tax introduced in 1991 as an example, explain a Pigouvian tax to correct negative externalities.
items.answer: Sweden taxes carbon at around SEK 1,200 (about $120) per tonne, one of the highest rates in the world; emissions fell by over 30% between 1990 and 2020 while GDP grew strongly. The tax raised the private cost of fossil fuels towards their social cost, encouraging switching to biomass and other low-carbon energy.
items.markingKey: Context (Sweden taxes carbon at around SEK 1,200 (about $120) per tonne, one of the highest rates in the world; emissions fell by over 30% between 1990 and 2020 while GDP grew strongly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The tax raised the private cost of fossil fuels towards their social cost, encouraging switching to biomass and other low-carbon energy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a Pigouvian tax to correct negative externalities.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Carbon taxes are the most effective policy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
items.answer: Carbon taxes are efficient in principle and effective in practice where politically sustainable, but they work best alongside regulation, subsidies for clean technology and international cooperation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: internalise the externality using the price mechanism; allow emissions to be cut where cheapest; raise revenue that can be recycled (British Columbia). Arguments against: difficult to set at the correct level; regressive and politically unpopular (France's gilets jaunes, 2018); may cause carbon leakage to countries without taxes; inelastic demand for fuel limits the short-run effect. Supported judgement: Carbon taxes are efficient in principle and effective in practice where politically sustainable, but they work best alongside regulation, subsidies for clean technology and international cooperation.

items.stem: Explain why regulation may be preferred to taxation for some negative externalities.
items.answer: If the harm is severe or the externality is dangerous (e.g. toxic chemicals), a ban or strict limit guarantees the outcome, whereas a tax allows the activity to continue for those willing to pay.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the harm is severe or the externality is dangerous (e.g. toxic chemicals), a ban or strict limit guarantees the outcome, whereas a tax allows the activity to continue for those willing to pay. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Banning a good is always the best way to deal with a negative externality." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bans can create black markets, remove benefits that consumers value and are costly to enforce; taxes or permits may achieve the optimum more efficiently.
items.markingKey: Bans can create black markets, remove benefits that consumers value and are costly to enforce; taxes or permits may achieve the optimum more efficiently. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A coal power station in poland produces 1000 MWh of electricity per day, where MPB = MPC. Each unit causes pollution costing local residents $12 (constant marginal external cost). At the social optimum output would be 850. Calculate the welfare loss per day, state the Pigouvian tax per unit and the daily revenue it would raise.
items.answer: Welfare loss $900; tax $12 per unit; revenue $10,200

items.stem: Explain the externality caused by congestion when drivers enter central London, and how the congestion charge (introduced 2003) tries to correct it.
items.answer: Each driver adds to delays and pollution for others (negative consumption externality, MSB < MPB); the daily charge raises the private cost of driving into the zone, reducing journeys towards the optimum.
items.markingKey: Each driver adds to delays and pollution for others (negative consumption externality, MSB < MPB); the daily charge raises the private cost of driving into the zone, reducing journeys towards the optimum.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "direct provision"?
options: Government information campaigns that increase awareness of the benefits of a good, shifting MPB towards MSB
The extra cost to producers of producing one more unit, shown by the supply curve
A cost or benefit arising from production or consumption that affects third parties and is not reflected in the market price
The government itself supplies a good or service, often free at the point of use, to increase consumption
items.answer: The government itself supplies a good or service, often free at the point of use, to increase consumption
items.markingKey: D. "direct provision" is the government itself supplies a good or service, often free at the point of use, to increase consumption.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Goods with positive externalities are over-consumed because they are good for people." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Because decision-makers ignore the external benefits, goods with positive externalities are under-consumed relative to the social optimum.
items.markingKey: Because decision-makers ignore the external benefits, goods with positive externalities are under-consumed relative to the social optimum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between direct provision and a subsidy.
items.answer: A subsidy lowers the price of a good produced by private firms; direct provision means the government itself supplies it, often free at the point of use.
items.markingKey: A subsidy lowers the price of a good produced by private firms; direct provision means the government itself supplies it, often free at the point of use. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a city like Bogotá might subsidise bicycle-sharing schemes.
items.answer: Cycling creates positive externalities (less congestion, pollution and better public health) not considered by individual users, so MSB > MPB; a subsidy lowers the price, increasing use towards the optimum.
items.markingKey: Cycling creates positive externalities (less congestion, pollution and better public health) not considered by individual users, so MSB > MPB; a subsidy lowers the price, increasing use towards the optimum.

items.stem: "Making healthcare free removes all market failure in healthcare." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Free provision increases consumption but may cause over-use, waiting lists and a large fiscal burden; asymmetric information and moral hazard remain.
items.markingKey: Free provision increases consumption but may cause over-use, waiting lists and a large fiscal burden; asymmetric information and moral hazard remain. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Subsidies are the most effective way to correct positive externalities."
items.answer: Subsidies are often effective but must be well targeted and combined with other tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower price and raise quantity towards the optimum; flexible and targeted. Arguments against: cost to taxpayers and opportunity cost; difficult to set the right subsidy; firms may become dependent; information campaigns and regulation can be cheaper. Supported judgement: Subsidies are often effective but must be well targeted and combined with other tools.

items.stem: Define the term "positive externality of production".
items.answer: An external benefit created by producers for third parties, such as a firm training workers who later work elsewhere, so MSC < MPC

items.stem: Each of the 5,000 university places bought in a free market provides a constant external benefit of $30 to third parties. A ministry of education estimates the socially optimal quantity is 5,500. Calculate the welfare loss, the subsidy per unit needed and the total cost of the subsidy at the optimum.
items.answer: Welfare loss $7500; subsidy $30 per unit; cost $165,000

items.stem: Using a diagram, explain why vaccinations are under-consumed in a free market and evaluate the use of a subsidy to correct this.
items.answer: Diagram: MPB below MSB, MPC = MSC; market Qm < Q*; welfare loss triangle. Subsidy lowers price, increases quantity; evaluation: cost, measurement of external benefit, other policies (free provision, mandates, information), equity.
items.markingKey: Diagram: MPB below MSB, MPC = MSC; market Qm < Q*; welfare loss triangle. Subsidy lowers price, increases quantity; evaluation: cost, measurement of external benefit, other policies (free provision, mandates, information), equity.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sustainability"?
options: The extra benefit to consumers from consuming one more unit of a good, shown by the demand curve
A legal limit on the quantity of fish that a country, firm or boat may catch in a period
A tax on a good equal to the marginal external cost, designed to make producers or consumers internalise the externality
Using resources in a way that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
items.answer: Using resources in a way that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
items.markingKey: D. "sustainability" is using resources in a way that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

items.stem: Distinguish between a carbon tax and tradable permits.
items.answer: A carbon tax sets the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust, giving price certainty; tradable permits set the quantity of emissions and let the price adjust, giving certainty about the environmental outcome.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax sets the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust, giving price certainty; tradable permits set the quantity of emissions and let the price adjust, giving certainty about the environmental outcome. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why common pool resources are over-used.
items.answer: Because no one can be excluded, each user takes as much as is privately beneficial; the cost of depleting the stock is shared by all users and future generations, so the resource is used beyond sustainable levels.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Because no one can be excluded, each user takes as much as is privately beneficial; the cost of depleting the stock is shared by all users and future generations, so the resource is used beyond sustainable levels. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

The Amazon rainforest lost an estimated 13,000 km² of forest in the year to July 2021, the highest in 15 years, as land was cleared for cattle ranching and soy. Deforestation alerts fell by about 50% in 2023 after Brazil increased enforcement against illegal clearing.
— Extract based on data from Brazil's INPE satellite monitoring

Using the extract, explain why the Amazon is an example of a common pool resource problem and how government action affected the outcome.
items.answer: Forest is rivalrous (land cleared is lost) and hard to exclude people from; individual ranchers gain from clearing while the costs (biodiversity, carbon) are shared globally – tragedy of the commons. Stronger enforcement (regulation) reduced clearing.
items.markingKey: Forest is rivalrous (land cleared is lost) and hard to exclude people from; individual ranchers gain from clearing while the costs (biodiversity, carbon) are shared globally – tragedy of the commons. Stronger enforcement (regulation) reduced clearing. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how a cap-and-trade scheme sets the price of pollution permits, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: price of permits on the vertical axis, quantity of permits (emissions) on the horizontal; supply is vertical at the cap set by the government; demand by firms slopes down. The equilibrium permit price P1 is where demand meets the cap. Tightening the cap shifts supply left, raising the permit price and giving firms stronger incentives to cut emissions; higher demand from economic growth raises price without raising emissions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: price of permits on the vertical axis, quantity of permits (emissions) on the horizontal; supply is vertical at the cap set by the government; demand by firms slopes down. The equilibrium permit price P1 is where demand meets the cap. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Common pool resources can only be protected by government intervention.
items.answer: Government action is often necessary, but community management and property rights can be effective, especially for local resources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: regulation, quotas and taxes needed to limit use; international agreements need governments. Arguments against: Ostrom: communities can self-govern resources successfully; property rights (ITQs) can create private incentives; firms and consumers (certification schemes) also help. Supported judgement: Government action is often necessary, but community management and property rights can be effective, especially for local resources.

items.stem: Define the term "fishing quota".
items.answer: A legal limit on the quantity of fish that a country, firm or boat may catch in a period

items.stem: A student claims that a carbon tax guarantees a specific reduction in emissions. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions; the reduction depends on how firms and consumers respond (PED). A cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions; the reduction depends on how firms and consumers respond (PED). A cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax (2008) as an example, explain a carbon tax as a sustainability policy.
items.answer: The province introduced a carbon tax starting at CAD 10 per tonne, with revenue returned through cuts in income and business taxes. The tax internalised part of the external cost of emissions while recycling revenue limited its regressive effect; fuel use per person fell relative to the rest of Canada.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of regulation to reduce a negative externality?
options: A ban on smoking in public places
items.answer: A ban on smoking in public places

items.stem: Which policy would shift the MPB curve to the right to correct under-consumption of a merit good?
options: An information campaign about the benefits of the good
items.answer: An information campaign about the benefits of the good
items.markingKey: D. Information raises consumers' perceived private benefit; a producer subsidy shifts supply.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a public good and a common pool resource.
items.answer: Both are non-excludable, but a common pool resource is rivalrous (one person's use reduces what is left), whereas a public good is non-rivalrous.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the social optimum and the market equilibrium.
items.answer: The market equilibrium is where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is where MSB = MSC. They coincide only if there are no externalities.
items.markingKey: The market equilibrium is where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is where MSB = MSC. They coincide only if there are no externalities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why research and development by firms can create positive externalities.
items.answer: Knowledge spills over to other firms and society: discoveries can be copied or built upon, raising productivity elsewhere, but the inventing firm does not receive payment for these benefits, so R&D is under-provided.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Australia's plain packaging and tobacco tax rises from 2012 shows policies to reduce negative consumption externalities.
items.answer: Australia introduced plain packaging and large annual tax increases; smoking rates among adults fell to around 11% by 2019. Combining higher prices with information and regulation reduced consumption of a demerit good with external costs.
items.markingKey: Context (Australia introduced plain packaging and large annual tax increases; smoking rates among adults fell to around 11% by 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to Rwanda's community-based health insurance (Mutuelles de Santé), explain how it illustrates government intervention to increase consumption of merit goods.
items.answer: Heavily subsidised insurance covers over 80% of the population, raising the use of clinics and vaccinations. Lower costs to households increased consumption of healthcare, generating private and external benefits.
items.markingKey: Context (Heavily subsidised insurance covers over 80% of the population, raising the use of clinics and vaccinations.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower costs to households increased consumption of healthcare, generating private and external benefits. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to government intervention to increase consumption of merit goods.

items.stem: Briefly describe the collapse of the Grand Banks cod fishery off Newfoundland and explain what it reveals about the tragedy of the commons.
items.answer: Decades of over-fishing led to a collapse of cod stocks; Canada imposed a moratorium in 1992 and about 30,000-40,000 people lost their jobs. Open access led each fleet to maximise its own catch, depleting the shared stock until it collapsed.
items.markingKey: Context (Decades of over-fishing led to a collapse of cod stocks; Canada imposed a moratorium in 1992 and about 30,000-40,000 people lost their jobs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Open access led each fleet to maximise its own catch, depleting the shared stock until it collapsed. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the tragedy of the commons.

items.stem: A factory in Hanoi dumps waste into a river used by fishermen. Identify the private cost, the external cost and explain why the market output is too high.
items.answer: Private cost: the factory's own costs of labour, materials etc.; external cost: lost fish catches and health damage; the factory ignores external costs (MPC < MSC), so it produces where MPB = MPC, above the optimum where MSB = MSC.
items.markingKey: Private cost: the factory's own costs of labour, materials etc.; external cost: lost fish catches and health damage; the factory ignores external costs (MPC < MSC), so it produces where MPB = MPC, above the optimum where MSB = MSC.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the welfare loss caused by a negative externality of production and how a Pigouvian tax can eliminate it.
items.answer: Diagram: MPB = MSB, MPC and MSC (MSC above MPC by the marginal external cost). Market Qm, Pm at MPB = MPC; optimum Q*, P* at MSB = MSC; welfare loss triangle between Q* and Qm. A tax equal to the external cost shifts MPC up to MSC; output falls to Q* and the welfare loss is removed.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: MPB = MSB, MPC and MSC (MSC above MPC by the marginal external cost). Market Qm, Pm at MPB = MPC; optimum Q*, P* at MSB = MSC; welfare loss triangle between Q* and Qm. A tax equal to the external cost shifts MPC up to MSC; output falls to Q* and the welfare loss is removed. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Identify one market-based and one non-market policy to increase the number of children receiving the measles vaccine.
items.answer: Market-based: subsidy or making vaccination free (cash incentives); non-market: information campaigns, legislation making vaccination a requirement for school entry.
items.markingKey: Market-based: subsidy or making vaccination free (cash incentives); non-market: information campaigns, legislation making vaccination a requirement for school entry.

items.stem: The permit price in an emissions trading scheme is $90 per tonne of CO₂. Firm A (a cement maker) can cut emissions at $25 per tonne and Firm D (an airline) at $110 per tonne. Each must reduce its emissions or hold permits for an extra 5,000 tonnes. State what each firm will do and calculate each firm's cost of compliance.
items.answer: Firm A (a cement maker): abate (cut emissions) and sell/not buy permits, cost $125,000; Firm D (an airline): buy permits rather than abate, cost $450,000
items.markingKey: Firm A (a cement maker): abatement $25 < permit $90 ⇒ abate (cut emissions) and sell/not buy permits; cost 25 × 5,000 = 125,000 [2]; Firm D (an airline): $110 > $90 ⇒ buy permits rather than abate; cost 90 × 5,000 = 450,000 [2]. Emissions are cut by the lowest-cost firm.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the concept of allocative efficiency (MSB = MSC) is of limited practical use because external costs cannot be measured accurately.
items.answer: Measurement is difficult, but the MSB = MSC framework remains essential for deciding the direction and approximate scale of intervention.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: external costs (health, climate) are hard to value in money; estimates vary widely (social cost of carbon). Arguments against: even approximate values improve policy (carbon prices); the framework shows the direction of correction; cost-benefit analysis is widely used. Supported judgement: Measurement is difficult, but the MSB = MSC framework remains essential for deciding the direction and approximate scale of intervention.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that government regulation is more effective than taxation in reducing negative externalities of consumption.
items.answer: Regulation is preferable when harms are severe and immediate; taxes are usually more efficient for widespread, moderate externalities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: bans and limits give certain outcomes (smoking bans); easy to understand. Arguments against: regulation is inflexible and costly to enforce; taxes raise revenue and change incentives continuously; black markets may develop under bans. Judgement: Regulation is preferable when harms are severe and immediate; taxes are usually more efficient for widespread, moderate externalities. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that subsidies are the most effective way to correct positive externalities.
items.answer: Subsidies are often effective but must be well targeted and combined with other tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower price and raise quantity towards the optimum; flexible and targeted. Arguments against: cost to taxpayers and opportunity cost; difficult to set the right subsidy; firms may become dependent; information campaigns and regulation can be cheaper. Judgement: Subsidies are often effective but must be well targeted and combined with other tools. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that common pool resources can only be protected by government intervention.
items.answer: Government action is often necessary, but community management and property rights can be effective, especially for local resources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: regulation, quotas and taxes needed to limit use; international agreements need governments. Arguments against: Ostrom: communities can self-govern resources successfully; property rights (ITQs) can create private incentives; firms and consumers (certification schemes) also help. Judgement: Government action is often necessary, but community management and property rights can be effective, especially for local resources. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "market failure"?
options: A legal limit on the quantity of fish that a country, firm or boat may catch in a period
The extra cost to society of producing one more unit, equal to MPC plus any marginal external cost
The failure of the market to allocate resources efficiently, so that social surplus is not maximised (MSB ≠ MSC at the market output)
A resource that is rivalrous but non-excludable, such as fish stocks, groundwater or forests, so it tends to be over-used
items.answer: The failure of the market to allocate resources efficiently, so that social surplus is not maximised (MSB ≠ MSC at the market output)
items.markingKey: C. "market failure" is the failure of the market to allocate resources efficiently, so that social surplus is not maximised (MSB ≠ MSC at the market output).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An external cost created by producers that harms third parties, such as pollution from a factory, so that MSC > MPC"?
items.answer: negative externality of production
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of negative externality of production.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The government itself supplies a good or service, often free at the point of use, to increase consumption"?
items.answer: direct provision
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of direct provision.

items.stem: Explain the difference between tradable permits and a carbon tax.
items.answer: A carbon tax sets the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust, giving price certainty; tradable permits set the quantity of emissions and let the price adjust, giving certainty about the environmental outcome.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax sets the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust, giving price certainty; tradable permits set the quantity of emissions and let the price adjust, giving certainty about the environmental outcome. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the social optimum and the market equilibrium.
items.answer: The market equilibrium is where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is where MSB = MSC. They coincide only if there are no externalities.
items.markingKey: The market equilibrium is where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is where MSB = MSC. They coincide only if there are no externalities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a cap-and-trade (tradable permit) scheme and a carbon tax.
items.answer: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the price of permits adjust in the market.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax fixes the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the price of permits adjust in the market. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila writes: "Making healthcare free removes all market failure in healthcare." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Free provision increases consumption but may cause over-use, waiting lists and a large fiscal burden; asymmetric information and moral hazard remain.
items.markingKey: Free provision increases consumption but may cause over-use, waiting lists and a large fiscal burden; asymmetric information and moral hazard remain. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why tradable permits reduce pollution at the lowest overall cost.
items.answer: Firms that can cut emissions cheaply do so and sell spare permits, while firms with high abatement costs buy permits; total emissions equal the cap, and reductions happen where they are cheapest.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Firms that can cut emissions cheaply do so and sell spare permits, while firms with high abatement costs buy permits; total emissions equal the cap, and reductions happen where they are cheapest. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between social costs and private costs.
items.answer: Private costs are borne by the producer or consumer making the decision; social costs are private costs plus external costs borne by third parties.
items.markingKey: Private costs are borne by the producer or consumer making the decision; social costs are private costs plus external costs borne by third parties. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Sweden's carbon tax introduced in 1991 shows a Pigouvian tax to correct negative externalities.
items.answer: Sweden taxes carbon at around SEK 1,200 (about $120) per tonne, one of the highest rates in the world; emissions fell by over 30% between 1990 and 2020 while GDP grew strongly. The tax raised the private cost of fossil fuels towards their social cost, encouraging switching to biomass and other low-carbon energy.
items.markingKey: Context (Sweden taxes carbon at around SEK 1,200 (about $120) per tonne, one of the highest rates in the world; emissions fell by over 30% between 1990 and 2020 while GDP grew strongly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The tax raised the private cost of fossil fuels towards their social cost, encouraging switching to biomass and other low-carbon energy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a Pigouvian tax to correct negative externalities.

items.stem: A student claims that Goods with positive externalities are over-consumed because they are good for people. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Because decision-makers ignore the external benefits, goods with positive externalities are under-consumed relative to the social optimum.
items.markingKey: Because decision-makers ignore the external benefits, goods with positive externalities are under-consumed relative to the social optimum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how individual transferable fishing quotas (ITQs) in Iceland and New Zealand help prevent the tragedy of the commons.
items.answer: The total allowable catch is limited; quotas give each holder a share they can trade, so fishers have an incentive to protect the stock (future quota value rises), reducing over-fishing.
items.markingKey: The total allowable catch is limited; quotas give each holder a share they can trade, so fishers have an incentive to protect the stock (future quota value rises), reducing over-fishing.

items.stem: Briefly describe air pollution from coal power in northern India and explain what it reveals about the divergence between MPC and MSC.
items.answer: Coal-fired power stations around Delhi contribute to severe air pollution linked to respiratory illness. Producers' costs exclude the health damage to residents, so MSC > MPC and too much electricity is generated from coal.
items.markingKey: Context (Coal-fired power stations around Delhi contribute to severe air pollution linked to respiratory illness.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Producers' costs exclude the health damage to residents, so MSC > MPC and too much electricity is generated from coal. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the divergence between MPC and MSC.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the over-consumption of a good with a negative consumption externality, such as cigarettes.
items.answer: Diagram: supply = MPC = MSC; MPB above MSB. Market at Qm where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC; Qm > Q* – over-consumption; welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Qm. Policies: tax, regulation (bans in public places), education.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: supply = MPC = MSC; MPB above MSB. Market at Qm where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC; Qm > Q* – over-consumption; welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q* to Qm. Policies: tax, regulation (bans in public places), education. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Singapore's SkillsFuture programme gives every citizen aged 25 and above a credit (initially S$500) to spend on approved training courses. The government argues that a more skilled workforce raises productivity across the economy.
— Extract based on information about Singapore's SkillsFuture scheme

Using the extract, explain why the government subsidises training.
items.answer: Training creates positive externalities (MSB > MPB): more productive workers benefit other firms and society, so individuals and firms under-invest; the credit lowers the private cost, increasing training towards the optimum.
items.markingKey: Training creates positive externalities (MSB > MPB): more productive workers benefit other firms and society, so individuals and firms under-invest; the credit lowers the private cost, increasing training towards the optimum. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax (2008) and explain what it reveals about a carbon tax as a sustainability policy.
items.answer: The province introduced a carbon tax starting at CAD 10 per tonne, with revenue returned through cuts in income and business taxes. The tax internalised part of the external cost of emissions while recycling revenue limited its regressive effect; fuel use per person fell relative to the rest of Canada.
items.markingKey: Context (The province introduced a carbon tax starting at CAD 10 per tonne, with revenue returned through cuts in income and business taxes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The tax internalised part of the external cost of emissions while recycling revenue limited its regressive effect; fuel use per person fell relative to the rest of Canada. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a carbon tax as a sustainability policy.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Market failure is so common that governments should intervene in most markets."
items.answer: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: externalities are widespread (energy, transport, food); information problems in health, finance. Arguments against: many markets work well without intervention; government failure is also common; intervention has administrative costs. Supported judgement: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets.

items.stem: Using a diagram, explain how a tax on petrol might correct the negative externality associated with its consumption, and discuss one limitation of this policy.
items.answer: Diagram: MPB, MSB below MPB, supply = MPC = MSC; market at MPB = MPC above optimum; tax reduces quantity towards Q* where MSB = MSC. Limitations: inelastic demand, regressive, hard to measure external cost, political opposition.
items.markingKey: Diagram: MPB, MSB below MPB, supply = MPC = MSC; market at MPB = MPC above optimum; tax reduces quantity towards Q* where MSB = MSC. Limitations: inelastic demand, regressive, hard to measure external cost, political opposition.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that direct government provision is the best way to increase consumption of merit goods.
items.answer: Direct provision is effective for basic merit goods such as primary education, but subsidies, regulation and information can complement it more efficiently.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: guarantees access for all (equity); can achieve large increases in consumption quickly; avoids reliance on private profit motives. Arguments against: high fiscal cost and opportunity cost; possible inefficiency and lack of choice; over-consumption and waiting lists when free; subsidies or vouchers may achieve similar results at lower cost. Judgement: Direct provision is effective for basic merit goods such as primary education, but subsidies, regulation and information can complement it more efficiently. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples.
